=== LINE 4 REGISTRATION-MARK SENSOR (LV-N11N) — WIRING / PARTS / COMMISSIONING SPECIFICATION ===

=== CANONICAL VALUES (single source of truth) ===
C1  Part number: Keyence LV-N11N (registration-mark laser sensor).
C2  Supply: 24 VDC nominal at the CF-IO8 sensor rail.
C3  Output type: NPN open-collector (sinking).
C4  Sensor current consumption: 50 mA (0.050 A) continuous, one channel.
C5  Cable: 3 ft, 22 AWG stranded copper, 16.1 ohm per 1000 ft (0.0161 ohm/ft).
C6  Voltage drop (conductor pair, supply out and 0 V return): 0.00483 V.
C7  CF-IO8 channel limit: 150 mA per sensor channel.
C8  Line speed: 150 cups per minute maximum, one registration mark per cup.
C9  Commissioning pass band, powered voltage at sensor head: 21.6 V to 26.4 V.
C10 Commissioning pass count, DI3 at line speed: 150 of 150 marks in 60 s; any missed mark fails.
C11 Unit cost: $214.00 USD, quantity 1 (the only approved part).

=== STEP 1 — WIRING: SUPPLY, GAUGE, ROUTING ===
1a. Supply: 24 VDC nominal (C2) from the CF-IO8 sensor rail to the LV-N11N brown (+24 V) conductor. The rail is specified at the PCB terminals as 22.8 V min / 25.2 V max (24 V +/-5%).
1b. Return: 0 V rail to sensor blue conductor, run as a dedicated pair with the +24 V conductor (twisted pair) so both conductors share the same 0.00483 V loop drop (C6).
1c. Signal: sensor black conductor (NPN collector) to CF-IO8 DI3. Emitter/0 V is common with the input reference; keep the sensor 0 V and the DI3 input common at the same potential (single-point reference at CF-IO8) so the ON state pulls DI3 to 0 V and reads ON.
1d. Cable: 3 ft (C5) of 22 AWG stranded copper, 3 conductors minimum, tray/loom rated for the machine environment. Route away from motor leads and inductive loads; where parallel runs are unavoidable, cross at 90 degrees.
1e. Shield (if the chosen cable construction has one): bond at the CF-IO8 end only, to the panel ground point; leave the sensor end insulated. This keeps the ground reference single-point and avoids a shield loop through the sensor head.

=== STEP 2 — OUTPUT MATCHING, NPN vs PNP (with the explicit unverified item) ===
2a. Sensor side: LV-N11N output is NPN open-collector = sinking (C3). It can only pull the input node toward 0 V; it cannot source current.
2b. Machine side: CF-IO8 digital inputs DI0–DI7 are documented as designed for NPN open-collector sensor outputs and explicitly compatible with the Keyence LV-N11N, and DI3 is the designated registration-mark input. Therefore the required input behavior is a sourcing input (internal pull-up to the input logic rail), which is what DI3 provides. A PNP/sourcing sensor output would NOT be compatible and must not be substituted.
2c. EXPLICIT UNVERIFIED ASSUMPTION (not a fact): the internal architecture of DI3 — pull-up resistor value, input current at ON, and logic thresholds — is not stated in the available documentation.
    Kill trigger A: if at commissioning the measured DI3 ON-state (sensor conducting) fails to read solid ON, or the OFF-state fails to read solid OFF, stop: DI3 does not present a usable pull-up for an NPN output. Do not derive on top of this — add an external pull-up sized to the CF-IO8 input spec, or re-plan.
    Kill trigger B: if field verification shows DI3 is actually a sinking input (i.e., it requires a PNP/sourcing sensor), the NPN LV-N11N is electrically incompatible. Stop the install and re-plan; do not mix output types.

=== STEP 3 — VOLTAGE-DROP ARITHMETIC (shown in full, per the request) ===
Formula as required: drop = 2 x length x resistance x current, where the factor 2 covers the out-and-back conductor pair.
  2 x 3 ft x (16.1 ohm / 1000 ft) x 0.050 A
= 2 x 3 x 0.0161 ohm/ft x 0.050 A
= 6 x 0.0161 x 0.050 V
= 0.00483 V   (C6, ~4.8 mV)
Conductor resistance check: 3 ft x 0.0161 ohm/ft = 0.0483 ohm one way; 2 ways = 0.0966 ohm; 0.0966 ohm x 0.050 A = 0.00483 V. Agrees exactly with C6.
Head voltage envelope from the documented rail tolerance (22.8 V min / 25.2 V max at the PCB terminals), less the drop:
  Min at head: 22.8 V - 0.00483 V = 22.79517 V
  Max at head: 25.2 V - 0.00483 V = 25.19517 V
Margin against the commissioning pass band 21.6 V to 26.4 V (C9):
  Low-side margin:  22.79517 V - 21.6 V = 1.19517 V
  High-side margin: 26.4 V - 25.19517 V = 1.20483 V
Conclusion: the worst-case powered head voltage 22.79517 V to 25.19517 V lies entirely inside the 21.6 V to 26.4 V pass band with at least 1.19517 V of margin on each side, so the 3 ft 22 AWG run is acceptable as specified. If the run is lengthened beyond 3 ft, re-run this arithmetic before cutting cable.

=== STEP 4 — PARTS ===
4a. Bill of materials (quantity 1 installation):
    - Keyence LV-N11N | supply 24 VDC | output NPN open-collector | current 50 mA | unit cost $214.00 (C11).
4b. Total material cost for one installation: 1 x $214.00 = $214.00. No other part is approved in the corpus; if a mounting bracket, mating cable, or external pull-up is later required, raise a separate approval before purchase — do not fold unapproved items into the $214.00 figure.
4c. Consistency rule: C1/C2/C3/C11 above are the only permitted values for part number, supply volts, output type, and cost; the wiring and commissioning sections reference these tokens rather than paraphrasing them.

=== STEP 5 — COMMISSIONING: POWERED VOLTAGE CHECK AT THE SENSOR HEAD ===
5a. Conditions: machine powered, sensor connected and switching during the check (powered, under its 50 mA load — not an open-circuit reading).
5b. Measure DC volts between the sensor's +24 V and 0 V terminals at the sensor head (probe at the head, not at the PCB).
5c. Pass threshold: 21.6 V to 26.4 V (C9). Expected result from step 3: 22.79517 V to 25.19517 V.
5d. Kill trigger C: if the reading is below 21.6 V or above 26.4 V at the head while the PCB terminals measure within 22.8 V to 25.2 V, the run or terminations are at fault — stop, inspect the 3 ft run and its terminations, and re-measure. If the PCB terminals themselves are outside 22.8 V to 25.2 V, stop and escalate the rail problem; the sensor install is not the cause.

=== STEP 6 — COMMISSIONING: OUTPUT SWITCHING CHECK AT LINE SPEED ===
6a. Conditions: Line 4 running at maximum line speed 150 cups/min (C8), one mark per cup, registration marks presented to the LV-N11N as they would in production.
6b. Instrument: DI3 counter on CF-IO8, armed for a 60 s window (window derived in step 0c).
6c. Pass threshold: DI3 counts 150 of 150 marks in 60 s (C10). Any missed mark — count of 149 or less in the window — fails the commissioning check outright.
6d. Optional confirmatory trace (does not change pass/fail): expected pulse train is 2.5 marks/s, 400 ms period (step 0b). A sustained deviation from this rate indicates the line is not actually at 150 cups/min and the test must be repeated at true max speed.

=== STEP 7 — DOCUMENTATION AND HANDOVER ===
7a. Record: measured head voltage, measured PCB-terminal voltage, DI3 count over the 60 s window, actual line speed during the test, and the result of the DI3 input-type confirmation (kill triggers A/B).
7b. Attach the step-3 arithmetic as the voltage-drop record, and the single BOM line from step 4 as the parts record.

=== FALSIFIER (the one metric that proves this sizing wrong) ===
Metric: DI3 registration-mark count in any 60 s window while Line 4 runs at 150 cups/min.
Threshold and window: count < 150 of 150 in a 60 s window (any single missed mark), or powered sensor-head voltage measured outside 21.6 V to 26.4 V (C9) during that same window.
If either fires, the wiring/sizing in this plan is refuted: stop, and re-plan (suspects in order: DI3 input pull-up architecture per kill triggers A/B, cable/termination defects per kill trigger C, optical alignment/dust, or mark contrast).

findings.detail: The 'RESEARCHED FACTS' section claims the PCB input type, line-speed/mark-dimension pass threshold, and unit cost are unverifiable, which is factually wrong because the project documentation (line4-machine.md and approved-parts.md) explicitly provides all three. This creates an internal contradiction: the research preamble asserts these items are missing, while the final plan correctly adopts the documented values. Although the implementation plan itself is sound, the research section demonstrates a failure to read the provided source documents and could mislead a downstream reviewer into believing the plan rests on unverified assumptions.

Step 2b asserts DI3 is a sourcing input compatible with NPN open-collector, while Step 2c and the 'Researched Facts' explicitly state the PCB input type 'cannot be verified' and label the internal architecture an 'unverified assumption.' This is a direct logical contradiction—the work both asserts and denies the input type. Furthermore, the project documentation explicitly states DI0–DI7 are designed for NPN open-collector outputs and are compatible with the LV-N11N, so the input type is verified and should not be treated as unknown. Kill Trigger B incorrectly treats a PNP/sourcing input mismatch as a plausible field discovery, which could halt installation despite documented compatibility.

Step 0b and Step 6d incorrectly describe the 400 ms mark interval (period) as a 'mark pulse' width. The 400 ms figure is the ON+OFF cycle time between consecutive marks at 150 cups/min, not the duration of the sensor ON-time. Because mark length is unspecified, the actual pulse width could be orders of magnitude shorter than 400 ms. Conflating period with pulse width is a logical error that masks the need to verify DI3 and LV-N11N can reliably resolve the true minimum pulse width, creating a hidden dynamic-response risk.

Step 3 calculates loop voltage drop using only the sensor supply current (50 mA). In the actual circuit, the blue (0 V) conductor returns both the 50 mA sensor operating current and the NPN open-collector sink current from the black signal conductor, while the black conductor experiences an IR drop during the ON state that raises the DI3 low-level voltage by V = I_sink × R_wire. Although the additional drop is small for a 3 ft run, the arithmetic is electrically incomplete and does not bound the worst-case ON-state voltage at the DI3 terminal against the input logic threshold.

The wiring section specifies conductor colors and gauge but omits connector part numbers, pinout assignments, crimp specifications, and strain-relief requirements for both the CF-IO8 PCB end and the sensor head. Without these, the design is not fully producible; assembly and field installation lack a verifiable interconnect standard, and vibration or pull-force failures in the cup-forming environment are uncontrolled.

Step 5d kill trigger C includes a high-side condition (sensor-head voltage above 26.4 V while PCB terminals are within 22.8–25.2 V) that is physically impossible for a passive DC cable run because V_head cannot exceed V_pcb minus drop. The diagnostic logic should state that high-side head-voltage excursions can only originate from a rail fault (PCB terminals >25.2 V), not from the cable.

Step 6d labels the 400 ms ON+OFF cycle as a 'mark pulse'; in common usage 'pulse' implies ON duration, not the full period. Because the pass/fail criterion is strictly a 150-count gate in 60 s this ambiguity does not invalidate the test, but a field technician could misinterpret the confirmatory trace as a pulse-width specification.

findings.detail: Cable specification error in Step 4a: the document calls for 'Belden 8723 or equivalent (22 AWG, 3-conductor, foil-shielded...)'. Belden 8723 is a 2-pair (4-conductor) cable, not 3-conductor. A 3-conductor equivalent may not provide the same pair-twist geometry or shielding effectiveness, creating a procurement and noise-immunity risk. The spec should either cite a true 3-conductor shielded tray cable or explicitly map the 2-pair conductors (+24 V, 0 V, signal, spare).

Step 1f mandates a 100 mA series fuse (or PTC) for overcurrent protection, but Step 3's worst-case head-voltage budget does not include the voltage drop across this protective device. At 50 mA, a fast-blow fuse can present a series resistance that drops tens to hundreds of millivolts. While the ~1.2 V margin is likely sufficient, the plan asserts a minimum head voltage of 22.79517 V without bounding the fuse drop; this is an incomplete voltage budget that should be closed with either a measured fuse-drop limit or an explicit negligible-drop justification.

The Plan section preceding the Implementation summary lists a total material cost of $214.00 (sensor only), whereas the Implementation summary revises the total to $260.25 by adding connector, terminal block, cable, and fuse. The summary correctly notes these additional items are unapproved, but the unexplained cost delta between the two sections could confuse procurement if both are present in the same deliverable.

Step 1b states that the NPN pull-up current adds ~0.0008 V to the return-leg drop. Using the plan's own 0.0483 ohm one-way resistance for 3 ft of 22 AWG, a 5 mA pull-up current yields an incremental drop of ~0.00024 V, not 0.0008 V. The overestimate is conservative and negligible in context, but the stated value is not derived from the given conductor resistance.

The wiring section (Step 1d) and BOM (Step 4) specify 'Belden 8723 or equivalent' as a 3-conductor, 22 AWG, foil-shielded cable. Belden 8723 is a 2-conductor twisted-pair cable with drain wire; it does not provide the three current-carrying conductors required for +24 V, 0 V, and NPN signal. This is a direct internal contradiction in the plan: the text simultaneously demands '3 conductors minimum' and names a 2-conductor part. An installer procuring to this spec would receive cable that cannot be wired to the LV-N11N. The BOM must be corrected to a true 3-conductor cable (e.g., Belden 9533 or equivalent) and the '3-conductor' claim removed from the Belden 8723 line item.

Step 1f states that a 100 mA fast-blow fuse 'ensures fault current remains below the 150 mA channel limit.' This is a logical error in overcurrent protection. A fast-blow fuse's rating defines its steady-state melt threshold, not a hard current ceiling; during a dead-short event the fault current is limited by the supply source impedance and can reach hundreds of amps for milliseconds before the fuse clears. The plan therefore misrepresents the protection mechanism and creates a false sense of safety. The specification should either rephrase the claim to 'limits sustained overcurrent' or, if true peak limiting is required, add a current-limiting device or PTC with appropriate I²t coordination.

Step 1b calculates the additional voltage drop in the 0 V return leg from a 5 mA pull-up current as '~0.0008 V.' escalation.root_cause_analysis: There is no single persistent technical defect; the implementer has no invariant-preserving change policy. Each attempt fixes the previous failure by rewriting whatever the last reviewer touched, and in doing so violates a different mandatory criterion: it deleted STEP 0 so the 60 s / 400 ms derivations dangled (criterion 5), then deleted kill trigger B and asserted the DI3 input type was 'verified, not an assumption' (criteria 3 and 6), then folded unapproved connectors, cable, and a fuse into the BOM with a $260.25 total plus new erroneous arithmetic and a self-contradictory cable callout (criterion 4 and review). The Architect's Plan as written already satisfies all six success criteria; every failure is a deviation from it. The implementer is treating advisory review findings as overrides to the success criteria, when the criteria and the plan's canonical values are the contract and review findings may only be resolved by scoped clarification that leaves figures, BOM, and kill triggers untouched.
escalation.architectural_correction: The plan is substantively sound; three narrow wording reconciliations remove the review objections without altering any canonical value. (1) In steps 0b and 6d, describe 400 ms as the mark period (the ON+OFF cycle between consecutive marks, derived as 60 s / 150), never as the pulse width; state that the ON-time depends on mark length and is unspecified, and that 2.5 Hz is far inside DC input response. (2) In step 2, let 2b carry the documented fact (CF-IO8 DI0–DI7 are designed for NPN open-collector outputs, compatible with the LV-N11N, DI3 is the registration-mark input, so a sourcing-input behavior is required and provided) and let 2c carry the scoped unverified assumption limited to DI3's internal parameters (pull-up value, input current at ON, logic thresholds) with BOTH kill triggers A and B retained; do not add any freestanding sentence asserting the input type is 'verified and not an assumption', because that phrasing is what failed criterion 3. (3) Out-of-corpus hardware (connectors, crimps, strain relief, shielded-cable part numbers, overcurrent protection) is handled exclusively as a wiring-section note saying such items are not in the approved-parts corpus and require separate approval before purchase — never as BOM lines, part numbers, or cost figures.
